## 0. Why this audit exists

Houston flagged Cabinet as a critical UI/UX reference point. Quote: "it is a managed agents competitor with a very nice ui/ux cleaner friendly view than ours currently that i really like it frankly feels so much more approachable and usable and has tons of the features that we actually need." Cabinet is NOT a scientific research competitor — it's a knowledge-base + agents + embedded apps OS for solo creators, startups, B2B, consulting, etc. But the **UI/UX bar Cabinet sets is the bar Hubify Labs needs to hit.**

## SECTION A — Marketing site, positioning, UX patterns

---

### A.1 — Cabinet's positioning (what they sell)

**The problem Cabinet solves:** Every time you start a new Claude session, it forgets everything. Your project context, your decisions, your research — gone. You keep re-explaining the same things.

**The solution:** "One knowledge base. AI agents that remember everything. Scheduled jobs that compound. Your team grows while you sleep."

**Elevator pitch (verbatim from homepage):** "Your knowledge base. Your AI team. A free and open-source AI-first startup OS where everything lives as markdown files on disk. No database. No vendor lock-in. No subscription. No trial. No paywall. Clone it, run it, and make it your own."

**Target users:** Solo founders, indie app creators, newsletter writers, freelance consultants, B2B sales teams, OSS maintainers. The unifying thread is the solo operator or very small team who wants AI that actually remembers their context.

**Tagline (footer):** "Humans define intent. Agents do the work. The knowledge base is the shared memory."

**Built by:** Hila Shmuel, former Engineering Manager at Apple, building Cabinet in public with the open-source community. GitHub: hilash/cabinet. ~903 stars at time of audit.

**Business model:** Fully free and open source (MIT license) right now. Cabinet Cloud (hosted version) is "coming soon" — first paid tier. No subscription, no trial clock on the self-hosted version.

**Key differentiators over Notion/Obsidian:** Files live on disk as markdown. No database. No lock-in. Fully self-hosted. AI agents have persistent memory because the KB *is* the memory.

---

### A.2 — The "Not another note-taking app" comparison

Cabinet's comparison section is titled "Not another note-taking app" and positions against three explicit competitors:

- **Obsidian** — "a markdown editor" (just notes, no agents, no scheduled jobs, no apps, no terminal)
- **Notion** — "a team wiki" (cloud lock-in, no AI agents, no local files, no agent scheduling)
- **Paperclip** — "orchestrates agents" (good at org charts, budgets, audit logs — but no knowledge base, no editor, no content layer)

Cabinet's differentiator claim, verbatim: "Cabinet is the only tool that combines a knowledge base, AI agents, and embedded apps in one self-hosted OS."

**Feature comparison table rows (Cabinet vs Obsidian vs Notion vs Paperclip):**
- Knowledge base / wiki
- Markdown files on disk
- Self-hosted / local-first
- AI agent orchestration
- Agent org chart / hierarchy
- Agent heartbeats / scheduling
- Agent budget controls
- Embedded HTML apps
- Web terminal (xterm.js)
- WYSIWYG editor
- PDF / CSV viewing & editing
- Git-backed version history
- Internal team chat
- Mission / task system
- Linked Git repos
- Audit logs
- No database required

Cabinet claims all checkmarks. Obsidian gets: KB/wiki, markdown on disk, self-hosted, WYSIWYG editor. Notion gets: KB/wiki, WYSIWYG editor. Paperclip gets: AI agent orchestration, agent org chart, agent budget controls, audit logs.

**The critical gap Cabinet names in each competitor:**
- vs Obsidian: "no AI agents, no scheduled jobs, no embedded HTML apps, no web terminal. Cabinet is a knowledge OS, not just a note editor."
- vs Notion: "Notion locks your data in their cloud... You own your data. You can grep it."
- vs Paperclip: "no knowledge base, no editor, no content layer. Cabinet gives your agents a brain to read and write to."

**Design principle (verbatim):** "If it feels like enterprise workflow software, it's wrong. If it feels like watching a team work, it's right."

### A.3 — Hero + features

**Hero structure:**

The hero is a dictionary-entry format — genuinely novel and memorable:

```
cabinet /ˈkab.ɪ.nət/ noun
1. A cupboard with shelves or drawers for storing or displaying items. "a filing cabinet"
2. politics The committee of senior ministers responsible for controlling government policy. "a cabinet meeting"
3. software An AI-first knowledge base where files live on disk and a team of AI agents helps you execute. "I asked my cabinet to research the market and draft the blog post"
origin — mid 16th century: from cabinet, diminutive of Old French cabine. definition 3 — 2026, open source.
```

**CTAs:** "Download for Mac" (primary, cocoa brown filled button with macOS icon) + "or $ npx create-cabinet my-startup" (secondary, inline terminal snippet)

**Above hero badge:** "free project · open source · self-hosted"

**Subheadline (h2):** "Your knowledge base. Your AI team."

**Below hero:** A full product screenshot showing the 3-pane layout (sidebar file tree + main editor + AI panel). Five trust chips: "Markdown on disk · Self-hosted · Git-backed · AI-native · Open source"

**Feature blocks (12 total, each h3 + one-liner):**
1. WYSIWYG + Markdown — Tiptap rich text, slash commands, toggle to raw markdown
2. AI Agents — CEO, Editor, Marketer; each has goals, skills, scheduled jobs
3. Embedded HTML Apps — drop index.html, renders as iframe; full-screen mode
4. Web Terminal — xterm.js + node-pty, full Claude Code CLI in the browser
5. File-Based Everything — no database, markdown on disk, drag-and-drop sidebar
6. Git-Backed History — every save auto-commits, full diff viewer, restore any point
7. Scheduled Jobs — cron-based agent automation, Reddit scout every 6 hours
8. Missions & Tasks — goals to missions to Kanban boards with progress bars
9. Internal Chat — team channels, @mention an agent to trigger a response
10. Full-Text Search — Cmd+K instant search, FlexSearch index rebuilt on every change
11. PDF & CSV First-Class — inline PDF renderer, editable CSV tables, auto-save to git
12. Linked Git Repos — .repo.yaml links KB folders to source code repos

**"The Shift" section:** Uses Andrej Karpathy quotes about LLM knowledge bases as social proof / intellectual framing. Cabinet maps each Karpathy workflow step (Data Ingest, IDE/Viewer, Q&A, Output, Automation) to a Cabinet feature. Very effective legitimacy move.

### A.4 — Install flow

Cabinet has a dedicated "Install Flow" section with the heading "See Cabinet start up in the terminal." Copy: "The install walkthrough is back. One command scaffolds the workspace, sets up your AI team, and gets Cabinet running locally."

The terminal block shows a simulated shell prompt: `cabinet ~ zsh` with the install command animated inside it.

**The three install paths offered:**
1. `npx create-cabinet my-startup` (primary, shown inline in hero and install section)
2. `npx create-cabinet@latest` (GitHub README version)
3. "Download for Mac" button (macOS `.dmg` or package)

**"From zero to AI team in 2 minutes" — 4-step numbered sequence:**
1. **Install & Run** — "One command. Next.js + daemon start. Your knowledge base is a /data directory on disk." Code: `npx create-cabinet my-startup`
2. **Answer 5 Questions** — "What's your company? What do you do? What are your goals? Cabinet builds your custom AI team."
3. **Watch Your Team Work** — "Agents create missions, write content, scout Reddit, review quality — all on schedule."
4. **Knowledge Compounds** — "Every agent run, every edit, every research session adds to the KB. Your system gets smarter every day."

**Tech stack (from README):** Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Tiptap, Zustand, xterm.js, node-cron. Two processes: Next.js dev server (port 3000) + cabinet-daemon.ts (port 3001, WebSocket + job scheduler + agent executor).

### A.5 — "Hire your AI team in 5 questions"

Section heading: "Hire your AI team in 5 questions"
Copy: "Answer 5 questions. A CEO agent appears. It suggests teammates. Each agent has goals, skills, and recurring jobs. You watch them work like watching a real team."

**6 agent cards shown on the marketing page (the "featured 6"):**

| Agent | Tier | Description | Recurring jobs (chips) |
|-------|------|-------------|----------------------|
| CEO Agent | Lead | Strategic planning, goal tracking, task delegation. Creates missions, coordinates the team. | Weekly report, Goal review |
| Editor | Specialist | KB content editing, formatting, linking. Maintains documentation quality. | Content review, Link checker |
| Content Marketer | Specialist | Blog posts, social media, newsletters. SEO-optimized content generation. | Reddit scout, Blog drafts |
| SEO Specialist | Specialist | Keyword research, site optimization, ranking analysis. | Keyword tracker, Competitor scan |
| Sales Agent | Specialist | Lead generation, outreach, pipeline tracking. | Lead scorer, Follow-up drafter |
| QA Agent | Specialist | Review, proofread, fact-check content across the KB. | Content audit, Broken link scan |

**Full agent library (from README) — 20 pre-built templates across departments:**
- Leadership: CEO, COO, CFO, CTO
- Product: Product Manager, UX Designer
- Marketing: Content Marketer, SEO Specialist, Social Media, Growth Marketer, Copywriter
- Engineering: Editor, QA Agent, DevOps Engineer
- Sales & Support: Sales Agent, Customer Success
- Analytics: Data Analyst
- Operations: People Ops, Legal Advisor, Researcher

**Critical terminology observation for Hubify Labs:**
- Cabinet uses **"CEO Agent"** for what Hubify calls the "Orchestrator." The tier is "Lead" vs "Specialist" for all subordinates. This is the exact mental model we should consider. Houston is evaluating renaming our Orchestrator to "CEO" — Cabinet proves this resonates with the target user.
- The "Lead" vs "Specialist" tier distinction is clean and intuitive. No jargon, no "orchestrator," no "director."
- Job chips are shown as small rounded badges directly on the card. Each agent has 2 chip labels showing their recurring scheduled tasks. This is a powerful "proof of work" pattern — users see immediately what each agent *does* autonomously.

### A.6 — "How people actually use Cabinet" use cases

Section heading: "How people actually use Cabinet"
Copy: "Knowledge base + agents + files. One OS for wildly different workflows."

**6 swipeable use-case cards (tabs at bottom: B2C App | B2B Sales | Newsletter | Consulting | Open Source | Startup OS):**

Each card has: emoji icon, persona label (e.g. "Solo Founder"), a bold headline, a first-person quote from a fictional user, and a live Cabinet UI mockup showing the activity panel for that use case.

| Card | Emoji | Persona | Headline |
|------|-------|---------|----------|
| Startup OS | 🚀 | Solo Founder | "Strategy, roadmap, market — one place." |
| B2C App | 📱 | Indie App Founder | "My app runs itself while I sleep" |
| B2B Sales | 💼 | Small Business Owner | "2,000 leads. One army of agents." |
| Newsletter | ✍️ | Solo Creator | "Monday morning. Newsletter writes itself." |
| Consulting | 🏢 | Freelance Consultant | "Every client. One brain." |
| Open Source | ⚙️ | OSS Maintainer | "Merge PR. Changelog writes itself." |

**Pattern:** Every card quote follows the same formula: *immediate problem situation* + *what Cabinet does automatically* + *the outcome you get without lifting a finger.* Example: "I use it to run my B2C app. The App Store listing is a markdown page I can update any time. I have an hourly Reddit scout that surfaces user complaints, and a weekly competitor job that crawls the market and dumps everything into /market/competitors/. I wake up to a briefing."

**The UI mockups embedded in each card** show the "Activity — last 24h" panel for that use case: Cabinet workspace name, active agents, file tree, and a sample document updated by the agent. This makes the abstract concrete — users see exactly what the output looks like for their workflow.

**Hubify Labs takeaway:** Our marketing site has no use-case section at all. Cabinet's 6-card format is a direct conversion driver. We need an equivalent showing: Scientific Research (paper pipeline), Physics Experiment (anomaly detection), Literature Review, Grant Application, Data Analysis (MCMC), and Collaboration.

**Hubify Labs implication:** We should add a visible "Hubify Cloud — coming soon" waitlist block to our own marketing site immediately. Creates the funnel before the product ships.

### A.8 — Color palette + visual style

Cabinet uses a warm cream/beige/cocoa palette. The exact CSS custom properties, extracted live from the page:

| Token | Hex | Usage |
|-------|-----|-------|
| `--bg` | `#faf6f1` | Page background (warm off-white, not pure white) |
| `--bg-warm` | `#f3ede4` | Section backgrounds, subtle panels |
| `--bg-card` | `#ffffff` | Card/surface background |
| `--bg-card-hover` | `#fbf8f4` | Card hover state |
| `--bg-terminal` | `#2c2520` | Terminal block (dark cocoa, not pure black) |
| `--text-primary` | `#3b2f2f` | Headings, body copy (dark brown, not black) |
| `--text-secondary` | `#6b5b4f` | Secondary labels, descriptions |
| `--text-tertiary` | `#a89888` | Tertiary text, metadata |
| `--text-muted` | `#d4c8bb` | Disabled/muted states |
| `--accent` | `#8b5e3c` | Primary buttons, active states (cocoa brown) |
| `--accent-light` | `#a0714d` | Hover state on accent |
| `--accent-warm` | `#7a4f30` | Pressed/active on accent |
| `--accent-bg` | `#f5e6d3` | Accent-tinted backgrounds (tag chips, badges) |
| `--accent-bg-subtle` | `#faf2ea` | Very subtle accent wash |
| `--border` | `#e8ddd0` | Default borders |
| `--border-light` | `#f0e8dd` | Light/subtle borders |
| `--border-dark` | `#d4c4b0` | Emphasized borders |

**CTA button:** Background `#8b5e3c` (cocoa brown), text `#ffffff`. No gradients. Flat, warm.

**Overall visual description:** The entire site feels like aged parchment. The background is not white — it is warm cream `#faf6f1`. Text is not black — it is dark brown `#3b2f2f`. The accent is not blue or green — it is cocoa/terracotta `#8b5e3c`. This creates a "handcrafted knowledge archive" feeling that is fundamentally different from the cool-gray SaaS default. The dark terminal blocks (`#2c2520`) provide just enough contrast to break the warmth without destroying the aesthetic.

**No other accent colors visible on the marketing page.** Cabinet avoids the mistake of using multiple accent colors. The brown does all the lifting.

### A.9 — Typography

Cabinet uses four typefaces, loaded as Next.js font modules (all Google Fonts):

| Role | Font | Class in HTML |
|------|------|---------------|
| Large hero headings (h1) | **Instrument Serif** | `instrument_serif_*` |
| Body, UI, most headings (h2+) | **Inter** (variable) | `inter_*` |
| Code blocks, terminal, monospace | **JetBrains Mono** | `jetbrains_mono_*` |
| (Also loaded, minor use) | **Source Serif 4** | `source_serif_4_*` |

**Observed from computed styles:**
- `h1`: `"Instrument Serif"` then Georgia then serif (used for the hero dictionary entry and section hero headings)
- `h2` and body: `Inter` then system-ui then sans-serif (clean, readable, modern)
- `code`/`pre`: `"JetBrains Mono"` then Courier New then monospace (code blocks, terminal commands)

**Typography system summary:** Instrument Serif for emotional/brand moments. Inter for everything functional. JetBrains Mono for code. This is a clean 3-font stack with a clear hierarchy. The serif-for-hero creates warmth and distinction. The Instrument Serif + warm brown combination is the core of Cabinet's approachable personality.

**For Hubify Labs:** Our current typography uses Newsreader + Inter + JetBrains Mono. Newsreader is a reasonable analogue to Instrument Serif — both are display serifs. We should evaluate whether Instrument Serif better serves the "approachable knowledge archive" feeling, or whether Newsreader is sufficient if paired with the Cabinet color palette.

### A.10 — UI patterns to STEAL for Hubify Labs

Specific patterns from Cabinet we should implement:

- **Dictionary-entry hero** — Leading with a playful lexicographic definition of your product name creates instant brand personality and breaks the SaaS template. Hubify Labs could use the word "Lab" or "Hubify" in this format.

- **Warm cream default light mode** — Background `#faf6f1` (not white), text `#3b2f2f` (not black), accent `#8b5e3c` (cocoa, not blue/green). This palette is the single biggest differentiator in feel vs every other tool in the category. Houston specifically called this out. Ship it.

- **"Watching a team work" frame for agents** — Cabinet describes its agents by what they *do on schedule*, not what capabilities they have. Each agent card shows real job outputs in a simulated activity panel. Frame our agents the same way: "here's what your Orchestrator did yesterday."

- **Use-case carousel with embedded UI mockups** — 6 swipeable cards, each with a persona, quote, and live-looking UI screenshot. The mockup makes it concrete. Users can immediately see if Cabinet fits their workflow. We need this for Hubify Labs' scientific workflows.

- **Lead/Specialist agent tier system** — Simple two-level hierarchy. CEO Agent = Lead. Everything else = Specialist. No jargon. Consider adopting this for our agent hierarchy instead of Director/Orchestrator/Lead.

- **Activity feed as social proof** — Each use-case card shows "Activity — last 24h" as a live-feeling panel with file paths, agent actions, timestamps. This is not a real data panel — it is a designed mockup. But it communicates "your agents are always working" powerfully.

- **"Knowledge Compounds" 4-step sequence** — Steps 1-4 with large bold numbering (01-04). The final step is always about compounding value over time, not just what the product does today. This is a growth narrative baked into onboarding copy.

- **Karpathy quote legitimization** — Cabinet uses a specific, credible expert (Karpathy) and maps their exact workflow description to Cabinet features. Hubify Labs should do the equivalent with a cosmology or scientific discovery thought leader.

- **Embedded terminal mockup in install section** — Showing the actual shell prompt with the npx command inside a styled terminal block makes the install feel real and achievable. We should show `npx create-hubify` or equivalent.

- **"No subscription. No trial. No paywall."** — The explicit triple denial of pricing friction in the hero subhead is highly effective for OSS-first products. We should use equivalent copy.

- **Flat cocoa CTA buttons** — No gradients, no glow, no shadows. Solid warm brown `#8b5e3c` with white text. Clean and warm simultaneously.

- **Comma-separated trust chips** — "Markdown on disk · Self-hosted · Git-backed · AI-native · Open source" in one line below the hero. We should add our equivalent: "250+ datasets · Multi-model review · Local + cloud · Scientific-grade · Open source."

### A.11 — What Hubify Labs already has that Cabinet doesn't

- **Multi-lab framework** — Cabinet is single-workspace (one Cabinet instance = one project). Hubify Labs supports multiple independent labs in one account, each with its own agents, datasets, and privacy controls. This is a fundamental architecture advantage.

- **Cross-provider peer review** — Cabinet uses whichever AI provider you configure (Claude Code CLI or Codex CLI). It has no multi-model review pipeline. Hubify Labs mandates non-Anthropic sub-agents (GPT, Gemini, Grok, Perplexity) for cross-model peer review. No echo chamber. This is a core scientific discovery feature Cabinet cannot replicate without deep product rethinking.

- **24/7 always-on Fly.io orchestrator** — Cabinet's agents run via cron on your local machine. They stop when your laptop sleeps. Hubify's orchestrator runs on Fly.io machines continuously. Cabinet is invocation-based (jobs run on schedule but require the daemon to be up). Hubify is always-on.

- **Scientific Discovery Platform positioning** — Cabinet is a generic creator/startup OS. It has no concept of datasets, MCMC chains, anomaly detection, spectral analysis, or paper publishing. Hubify Labs is built specifically for scientific research: 250+ database connectors, 200+ scientific data formats, Houston Method v2 completion protocol, arxiv publish pipeline.

- **250+ database connectors + 200+ scientific data formats** — Cabinet's data model is "files on disk." Hubify Labs integrates directly with scientific survey databases (DESI, SDSS, Planck, ACT, eROSITA), MCMC chain formats, spectroscopic data, and custom data ingestion pipelines.

- **Houston Method v2 completion protocol** — Every experiment requires: QC gate, scientific analysis, interpretation, cross-survey connection, site sync, queue expansion, backup. This is a structured scientific method baked into the agent workflow. Cabinet has no equivalent.

- **Lab Sovereignty Rule** — Hubify Labs enforces that lab data never leaves the lab boundary without explicit researcher consent. Cabinet is local-first (data stays on disk) but has no formal sovereignty framework.

- **Publish-ready loop** — Hubify's pipeline goes from raw data through agent analysis through paper draft through peer review through arxiv submission. Cabinet has no paper pipeline.

- **GPU compute integration** — Hubify Labs routes inference jobs to RunPod H200 pods / Modal for GPU-intensive work. Cabinet has no GPU concept.

### A.12 — What we should COPY immediately (top 5 priorities)

Ranked by impact-to-effort ratio:

**1. Warm cream light mode as the default theme**
Ship the Cabinet palette: `--bg: #faf6f1`, `--text-primary: #3b2f2f`, `--accent: #8b5e3c`. This is one CSS file change that transforms the feel of the entire product from "cool SaaS" to "warm knowledge archive." Houston specifically asked for this. Estimated effort: 2 hours. Impact: immediately closes the biggest visual gap.

**2. Use-case carousel with embedded UI mockups**
Build 6 swipeable cards for Hubify Labs' target personas: Cosmology Researcher, Data Scientist, Lab PI, Independent Researcher, PhD Student, Computational Scientist. Each card: persona label, bold headline, first-person quote, activity panel mockup showing an actual Hubify workflow. This is the missing "does this work for me?" conversion driver on our marketing site. Estimated effort: 1-2 days.

**3. Rename Orchestrator to "CEO Agent" (or evaluate carefully)**
Cabinet proves this terminology resonates with solo operators. "CEO Agent" communicates authority, coordination, and delegation better than "Orchestrator." The Lead/Specialist tier distinction is cleaner than Director/Orchestrator/Lead. However, for a scientific research platform, "PI Agent" (Principal Investigator) may be more resonant than "CEO Agent." Evaluate: CEO Agent vs PI Agent vs Research Lead. Estimated effort: terminology change + copy update, 1-2 hours.

**4. "Hubify Cloud — coming soon" waitlist block**
Add a visible waitlist section to our marketing site mirroring Cabinet's pattern: heading, 3 benefit chips (No setup / Hosted for you / Multi-lab sync), CTA button linking to a Tally or typeform. Captures early adopters before the product launches. Estimated effort: 1-2 hours.

**5. Agent job chips on agent cards**
Every agent card in our UI should show 2-3 chip badges displaying its recurring scheduled tasks. "Weekly anomaly sweep · Cross-survey correlation · Nightly backup" on the Orchestrator card. "Dataset pull · QC gate · Chain convergence check" on the MCMC Agent card. This makes agents feel alive and productive rather than dormant configuration screens. Estimated effort: 1 day.

```
│   ├── lib/              # Business logic
│   │   ├── agents/       # Agent runtime, persona manager, conversation runner, providers
│   │   ├── storage/      # File I/O, path utils, page-io (read/write .md files)
│   │   ├── markdown/     # to-html, to-markdown converters
│   │   ├── chat/         # Chat API integration
│   │   ├── git/          # Git integration (simple-git)
│   │   ├── jobs/         # Job scheduling logic
│   │   ├── runtime/      # Runtime config (Electron vs web detection)
│   │   └── system/       # SQL + file migrations
│   ├── types/            # Shared TypeScript types
│   └── middleware.ts     # Next.js middleware (auth redirect)
├── server/               # Background daemon process (separate from Next.js)
│   ├── cabinet-daemon.ts # Unified daemon: PTY/WebSocket + job scheduler + chokidar file watcher
│   ├── db.ts             # Daemon-side SQLite init
│   └── migrations/       # SQL migration files (001_initial.sql, ...)
├── electron/             # Electron main process (main.cjs)
├── data/                 # Default KB content (CLAUDE.md, getting-started/, cabinet-example/)
├── public/               # Static assets
├── scripts/              # Build scripts (prepare-electron-package, generate-release-manifest)
├── test/                 # Unit tests (update-system, provider tests)
├── next.config.ts
├── forge.config.cjs      # Electron Forge config
├── components.json       # shadcn/ui config
└── cabinet-release.json  # OTA update manifest
```

---

### B.3 — Tech stack

| Layer | Choice |
|---|---|
| Frontend framework | Next.js 16.2.1 (App Router, React 19) |
| Build tool | Next.js + Electron Forge for desktop |
| State management | Zustand 5 (4 stores: app, editor, tree, ai-panel) |
| Routing | Next.js App Router + custom hash-based client routing (`useHashRoute`) |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS v4 + shadcn/ui + `tw-animate-css` + CSS custom props (oklch color space) |
| Rich text editor | TipTap v3 (Tiptap React + StarterKit + 10 extensions) |
| Terminal emulator | xterm.js (@xterm/xterm v6) over WebSocket PTY (node-pty) |
| Backend | Next.js API routes (server-side in the same Next.js process) |
| Background daemon | Separate Node.js process (`cabinet-daemon.ts`) via `tsx` |
| Data storage | Markdown files on disk (the KB) + SQLite (`better-sqlite3`) for conversations, jobs, metadata |
| File watching | chokidar v5 (daemon watches the data dir, pushes `tree_changed` SSE events) |
| Search | Custom file-system search (gray-matter frontmatter parse + substring match); flexsearch in deps but not primary |
| Agent runtime | Claude Code CLI and/or Codex CLI via node-pty PTY sessions |
| Desktop shell | Electron (electron-forge) — packages the Next.js app into an Electron wrapper |
| Icon library | Lucide React |
| Markdown parsing | unified + remark-gfm + rehype; gray-matter for frontmatter |

### B.4 — The 3-pane layout (sidebar + main + AI editor)

**File:** `src/components/layout/app-shell.tsx`

The layout is implemented as a single `AppShell` component with three sibling sections in a `flex h-screen` container:

```tsx
<div className="flex h-screen bg-background text-foreground">
  <Sidebar />                            // left pane
  <div className="flex-1 flex flex-col overflow-hidden">
    <main>{renderContent()}</main>       // main pane (editor/agents/settings)
    {terminalOpen && <TerminalTabs />}   // bottom drawer (terminal)
    <StatusBar />
  </div>
  {!aiPanelCollapsed && <AIPanel />}     // right pane (AI editor)
</div>
```

**Sidebar resizing:** Implemented with pointer events (not CSS resize) in `sidebar.tsx` lines 147–175. A drag handle div on the right edge captures `pointerdown`, then global `pointermove`/`pointerup` listeners on `window` update a `sidebarWidth` state variable. Width is persisted in `localStorage` under key `cabinet-sidebar-width`. Min: 220px, max: 420px, default: 280px.

**Sidebar collapse:** Managed by `useAppStore` (`sidebarCollapsed: boolean`). When collapsed, the sidebar renders as a thin icon-rail (hover strip) and a `--sidebar-toggle-offset` CSS variable is set on the main pane so the header can shift left to compensate.

**AI panel collapse:** Also managed by `useAppStore` (`aiPanelCollapsed: boolean`). The AI panel is simply not rendered when collapsed — no animation. Fixed width: `w-[480px] min-w-[420px]`.

**Auto-collapse behavior:** When a node with type `"app"` is selected, both sidebar and AI panel auto-collapse to give the iframe full screen (`app-shell.tsx` lines 147–154).

---

### B.5 — The @ mention system

**File:** `src/components/ai-panel/ai-panel.tsx` (lines 75–262)

The mention system lives entirely in the AI panel's chat input textarea. Key implementation details:

**State:**
```tsx
const [showMentions, setShowMentions] = useState(false);
const [mentionQuery, setMentionQuery] = useState("");
const [mentionIndex, setMentionIndex] = useState(0);       // keyboard nav
const [allPages, setAllPages] = useState<FlatPage[]>([]);  // fetched on panel open
const [mentionStartPos, setMentionStartPos] = useState(0); // cursor pos of '@'
```

**Trigger detection** (`handleInputChange`, lines 240–262): On every keystroke, takes the text before the cursor, finds the last `@`, checks that the character before `@` is a space/newline/start-of-input, then checks that no space/newline has appeared after `@`. If all conditions pass, extracts the query string between `@` and cursor and opens the dropdown.

**Data source:** On panel open, fetches `/api/tree` (returns the full KB tree as JSON) and flattens it with `flattenTree()` into `{ path, title }` pairs.

**Filtering:** Simple `title.toLowerCase().includes(query)` — no fuzzy search.

**Dropdown:** Absolutely positioned above the textarea (`bottom-full`), `max-h-[200px]` scrollable, shows up to 10 results. Arrow keys + Enter/Tab to navigate/select. Escape to dismiss.

**Insertion** (`insertMention`, lines 215–238): Replaces the `@query` portion of the input with `@PageTitle ` (note trailing space), adds the page path to `mentionedPages[]` (a separate array), and restores cursor position. The `mentionedPages` array is sent as `mentionedPaths` in the POST body when the user submits.

**Context injection:** On submit, the mentioned page paths are sent to `/api/agents/conversations`. The server-side `buildMentionContext()` function reads each page's markdown content and prepends it to the agent prompt as `--- Page Title (path) ---\ncontent`.

---

### B.6 — The inline AI editor

**Files:** `src/components/ai-panel/ai-panel.tsx`, `src/lib/agents/conversation-runner.ts`

The pattern is "Tell me how you'd like to edit this page" — a textarea in the right panel that spawns a Claude Code CLI session.

**Contract:**
1. User types instruction in the AI panel textarea (can use @ mentions for context).
2. On submit, POST to `/api/agents/conversations` with `{ source: "editor", pagePath, userMessage, mentionedPaths }`.
3. The API creates a conversation record in SQLite, builds a full prompt (agent persona + mentioned-page content + `buildCabinetEpilogueInstructions()`), then creates a daemon PTY session via `/api/daemon` (WebSocket to `cabinet-daemon.ts`).
4. The daemon spawns the CLI provider (Claude Code: `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`) in the `pagePath`'s directory as the working directory.
5. The conversation ID is returned to the frontend, which adds it to `editorSessions` in the AI panel store.
6. A `WebTerminal` component (xterm.js) connects to the daemon WebSocket session and streams live output.
7. When the CLI process exits, `handleSessionEnd()` fires: marks session completed, reloads the page content (so edits made by Claude appear in the editor), calls `loadPastSessions()` to refresh history.

**Epilogue protocol:** The agent is instructed to end its response with a ` ```cabinet ` code block containing `SUMMARY:`, `CONTEXT:`, and `ARTIFACT:` fields. The daemon parses this via `parseCabinetBlock()` and stores summary/artifacts in SQLite.

**Reconnect:** Sessions survive page navigation — hidden `WebTerminal` instances are kept mounted (in a 0-width div) for sessions on other pages so the WebSocket stays alive.

---

### B.7 — The PDF reader

**File:** `src/components/editor/pdf-viewer.tsx`

Cabinet's PDF viewer is intentionally minimal — it delegates entirely to the browser's native PDF renderer via an `<iframe>`:

```tsx
<iframe src={`/api/assets/${path}`} className="flex-1 w-full border-0" title={title} />
```

No PDF.js. No thumbnails, zoom controls, page navigator, or search. Just the browser's built-in PDF viewer in a full-height iframe. The `/api/assets/[...path]` route serves the file bytes with appropriate `Content-Type`. An "Open in new tab" button calls `window.open(pdfSrc, "_blank")`.

Type detection in `app-shell.tsx`: if a `TreeNode` has `type: "pdf"` or the path ends in `.pdf`, `PdfViewer` is rendered. Cabinet also handles `.csv` files with a `CsvViewer` and arbitrary HTML directories as embedded iframes (`WebsiteViewer`).

---

### B.8 — Agent system

**Files:** `src/lib/agents/persona-manager.ts`, `src/lib/agents/conversation-runner.ts`, `src/lib/agents/provider-interface.ts`, `src/lib/agents/providers/claude-code.ts`, `src/lib/agents/providers/codex-cli.ts`

**Agent definition format:** Agents are markdown files with YAML frontmatter, stored in `{DATA_DIR}/.agents/{slug}/index.md`. The frontmatter schema (`AgentPersona`) includes: `name`, `role`, `provider` (id string), `heartbeat` (cron expression), `budget` (max heartbeats/month), `active`, `workdir`, `focus` (string array), `tags`, `emoji`, `department`, `type`, `goals`, `channels`, `workspace`. The markdown body is the agent's system prompt.

**Orchestration model:** There is no central orchestrator agent. Routing is task-based: the user selects which agent to send a message to, or the editor AI panel always uses the "editor" agent slug. The "CEO Agent" seen in the sidebar is just a persona with slug `ceo` — it has no special routing logic over other agents.

**Provider abstraction:** An `AgentProvider` interface (`provider-interface.ts`) defines the contract for CLI vs API providers. Currently two providers are implemented:
- `claude-code.ts`: Spawns `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` as a PTY session.
- `codex-cli.ts`: Spawns the OpenAI Codex CLI.

The provider to use is configurable per-agent in frontmatter (`provider: "claude-code"` or `"codex"`), with a runtime default.

**Heartbeat system:** `persona-manager.ts` reads each agent's cron expression and runs periodic autonomous tasks. The daemon (`cabinet-daemon.ts`) hosts the cron scheduler. Heartbeat state (last run, next run, runs used vs budget) is tracked in SQLite.

**Claude Code integration in chat pane:** Yes — the `WebTerminal` in the AI panel IS a live Claude Code CLI session. The terminal pane at the bottom is also xterm.js, and users can launch additional Claude Code sessions from there.

---

### B.9 — Data model

**Pages (knowledge base):** Stored as markdown files on the filesystem inside `DATA_DIR` (configurable; defaults to `./data` in dev, to a user data directory in Electron). Each page is either a `.md` file (leaf) or a directory containing `index.md`. Frontmatter schema:

```typescript
interface FrontMatter {
  title: string; created: string; modified: string;
  tags: string[]; icon?: string; order?: number; dir?: "ltr" | "rtl";
}
```

**TreeNode** (in-memory, for sidebar): `{ name, path, type: "file"|"directory"|"website"|"app"|"pdf"|"csv", hasRepo?, frontmatter?, children? }`

**SQLite schema** (`server/migrations/001_initial.sql`): Stores conversations, conversation messages/transcripts, jobs, and metadata. Pages themselves are never in SQLite — the filesystem is the source of truth for KB content.

**Conversations** (`src/types/conversations.ts`): Each conversation has `id`, `agentSlug`, `title`, `trigger`, `status` ("running"|"completed"|"failed"|"cancelled"), `startedAt`, `completedAt`, `summary`, `artifacts[]`.

**Agents (personas):** Markdown files at `{DATA_DIR}/.agents/{slug}/index.md`. Not in SQLite — file system is authoritative.

**Jobs:** YAML files in `{DATA_DIR}/.jobs/`. Loaded by the daemon on startup, scheduled via `node-cron`.

**Wiki-links:** `[[Page Name]]` syntax handled by the TipTap `WikiLink` custom Mark extension. Stored in markdown as `[[Page Name]]`, converted to `<a data-wiki-link="true" href="#page:{slug}">` in HTML.

### B.10 — Color palette + theming (extracted from code)

**File:** `src/app/globals.css`, `src/lib/themes.ts`

Cabinet uses OKLCh color space throughout. The default theme is plain grayscale (no accent color):

**Light mode (`:root`):**
- Background: `oklch(1 0 0)` — pure white
- Foreground: `oklch(0.145 0 0)` — near-black
- Primary: `oklch(0.205 0 0)` — dark gray (used for active states)
- Muted/Accent: `oklch(0.97 0 0)` — very light gray
- Border: `oklch(0.922 0 0)` — light gray
- Sidebar: `oklch(0.985 0 0)` — off-white, slightly distinct from main bg
- Destructive: `oklch(0.577 0.245 27.325)` — red

**Dark mode (`.dark`):**
- Background: `oklch(0.145 0 0)`
- Primary: `oklch(0.922 0 0)` — light gray
- Border: `oklch(1 0 0 / 10%)` — white at 10% opacity
- Sidebar primary (dark): `oklch(0.488 0.243 264.376)` — blue accent (only colored element in default dark)

**Light/dark toggle:** Implemented via `next-themes` (`ThemeProvider` wraps the app). The CSS class `.dark` is applied to `<html>`. Custom themes use a `data-custom-theme` attribute on `<html>`.

**Multi-theme system** (`src/lib/themes.ts`): Cabinet ships ~10+ named themes (Claude, Midnight Ocean, Forest, Rose, etc.), each defined as an object with `vars: Record<string, string>` of CSS custom property overrides, plus `font` and `headingFont` Google Font strings. Themes are applied by injecting inline CSS vars on `<html>`. Notable named themes: "Claude" (warm orange-brown accent: `oklch(0.72 0.12 45)` ≈ `#cc785c`), "Midnight Ocean" (blue: `#5b8dee`).

**No hard-coded hex values in component files** — everything references CSS custom properties.

### B.11 — Components Hubify Labs should COPY directly (as patterns to reimplement)

These are patterns worth porting, not code to copy verbatim. Cabinet is MIT, but our stack and style differ.

1. **`AppShell` layout pattern** (`src/components/layout/app-shell.tsx`): The `renderContent()` switch that dispatches between editor/agents/settings/pdf/csv/website views based on selected node type is clean and extensible. Port the type-dispatch pattern for Hubify's main content area.

2. **Pointer-drag sidebar resize** (`src/components/sidebar/sidebar.tsx` lines 118–175): The `dragStateRef` + global `pointermove`/`pointerup` + `localStorage` persistence is exactly what Hubify needs. No third-party resize library — ~60 lines of vanilla pointer events.

3. **@ mention system in the chat textarea** (`src/components/ai-panel/ai-panel.tsx` lines 75–262): The full implementation — trigger detection on `@`, cursor position tracking via `selectionStart`, dropdown positioning with `bottom-full absolute`, keyboard navigation, insert-and-restore-cursor — is the canonical pattern for Hubify's chat @ mention. About 180 lines, all self-contained.

4. **`WikiLink` TipTap extension** (`src/components/editor/wiki-link-extension.ts`): A clean 66-line TipTap Mark extension with InputRule for `[[Page Name]]` syntax. If Hubify ever has an in-app markdown editor, this is the exact pattern to clone.

5. **`SearchDialog` Cmd+K pattern** (`src/components/search/search-dialog.tsx`): Keyboard shortcut registration in `useEffect` + debounced API search + keyboard navigation with `selectedIndex` state is the standard pattern Hubify should use.

6. **Agent persona YAML/markdown format** (`data/CLAUDE.md` + `persona-manager.ts`): Storing agent personas as `.md` files with YAML frontmatter is a simple, git-friendly, human-readable agent definition format. Hubify's agent definition format should be similar (or identical) for the local-first use case.

7. **`buildCabinetEpilogueInstructions()` convention** (`src/lib/agents/conversation-runner.ts` lines 35–42): Instructing agents to end with a structured ` ```cabinet ` code block containing `SUMMARY:`, `CONTEXT:`, `ARTIFACT:` is a clean structured-output trick that works without JSON mode. Hubify should adopt the same epilogue protocol for its agent runs.

8. **Multi-theme CSS variable system** (`src/lib/themes.ts`): Theme-as-a-record-of-CSS-vars is exactly the pattern Hubify should use. The OKLCh color space ensures perceptual consistency across themes.

9. **`AgentProvider` interface** (`src/lib/agents/provider-interface.ts`): The `AgentProvider` interface separating `"cli"` vs `"api"` providers with `buildSessionInvocation()` / `buildOneShotInvocation()` / `isAvailable()` / `healthCheck()` is a clean abstraction for supporting multiple AI CLI tools. Hubify should adopt this interface.

10. **SSE `tree_changed` live reload** (`src/components/layout/app-shell.tsx` lines 83–92): The app subscribes to `/api/agents/events` SSE and calls `loadTree()` on `tree_changed`. This is how Cabinet makes the sidebar update in real time when an agent modifies a file. Hubify should do the same for live lab/experiment state updates.

### B.12 — Architectural decisions Hubify Labs should adopt

**File-system as KB source of truth.** Cabinet never stores page content in SQLite — markdown files on disk are the authoritative store. SQLite is only for metadata and conversation history. This means the user's knowledge base is always a directory of `.md` files they can open in any editor, commit to git, or back up trivially. Hubify's research lab content should follow the same pattern.

**Daemon + Next.js split.** The long-running concerns (PTY sessions, cron jobs, chokidar file watching, WebSocket server) live in a separate `cabinet-daemon.ts` process, not inside Next.js API routes. This is the right architecture for Hubify too — Modal functions or Fly machines should host the long-running agent sessions, not serverless routes.

**Zustand for all UI state.** Four focused stores (app, editor, tree, ai-panel). Each store owns one domain. No prop-drilling, no Context for global state. Hubify should adopt Zustand for the same reasons.

**`AgentProvider` abstraction over CLI tools.** By abstracting Claude Code and Codex behind the same interface, Cabinet can swap providers without changing the UI. Hubify should build the same abstraction layer for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and future agent runtimes.

**Hash-based client routing inside a single Next.js page.** Cabinet's `useHashRoute` hook handles navigation between sections (agents, settings, specific page) via `window.location.hash`. This avoids full-page reloads in the Electron shell. Hubify should use the same pattern for the desktop app.

**OKLCh color space for all design tokens.** Better perceptual uniformity than HSL, cleaner dark/light theme math. Hubify should migrate from any remaining hex/HSL values to OKLCh.

---

### B.13 — What Cabinet does WORSE than Hubify Labs

**No real-time multi-agent coordination.** Cabinet's agents run as independent PTY sessions — there is no orchestrator routing work between agents, no shared message bus, no "tilldone" failure recovery, no cross-agent review. Each agent is siloed. Hubify's vision of director/orchestrator/lead/worker hierarchy is architecturally superior.

**No cloud sync or multi-device.** Cabinet is fully local-first with no sync layer. All data lives in one machine's filesystem. Hubify's Convex-backed cloud sync is a meaningful differentiator.

**No cross-model peer review.** Cabinet only ships two providers (Claude Code, Codex). There is no mechanism for a GPT-4 sub-agent to review a Claude output. Hubify's mandatory cross-model review is a genuine scientific-integrity feature Cabinet lacks.

**PDF viewer is a browser iframe shim.** Cabinet's "PDF reader" is literally `<iframe src={pdfUrl}>`. No annotations, no search, no page thumbnails, no zoom controls. Hubify's research use case demands a real PDF.js integration with annotation support.

**No GPU / compute integration.** Cabinet has no concept of attaching a compute resource (RunPod, Modal) to an agent. Hubify's "idle GPU is a violation" philosophy and its compute orchestration are features Cabinet will never have.

**Fragile file-system search.** Cabinet uses simple substring matching over frontmatter. No semantic search, no vector embeddings, no FlexSearch in production (it's in deps but not wired up for primary search). Hubify's research platform needs semantic search over papers and datasets.

**No activity feed / multi-agent visibility.** Cabinet has no equivalent of Hubify's color-coded multi-agent activity feed with lead takeover on worker failure. Cabinet's "jobs" view is a simple list — no real-time agent communication log.

**Electron packaging is fragile.** The `postinstall` script manually removes macOS quarantine flags from `node-pty` binaries. The Electron build requires a specific CI signing setup. Hubify should invest in a cleaner desktop shell or evaluate Tauri.
